findings.title: Provider selection is non-deterministic when order() ties; fail-fast on duplicates removed
findings.body: detectProvider now sorts discovered providers by CryptoProvider.order() descending and silently returns the first, removing the previous IllegalStateException thrown when more than one provider is on the classpath. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so whenever two of them are present (e.g. default crypto plus FIPS) the winner is decided solely by the non-deterministic ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order (the sort is stable), not by the order() value. In a FIPS deployment that can silently select the non-FIPS provider and downgrade cryptography, and genuine duplicate-provider misconfigurations that used to abort at startup now go unnoticed. The built-in providers need distinct deterministic order values, and equal-order duplicates should still fail rather than silently pick one.

findings.title: Adding order() as an abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: Adding `int order();` as an abstract method to the public CryptoProvider interface is a source- and binary-incompatible change for every third-party CryptoProvider implementation (custom providers, and the keycloak-client repo this code is later synced to). Such classes will no longer compile, and classes already compiled against an older version will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when CryptoIntegration.detectProvider invokes order(). It should be declared as a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) so existing implementations continue to work.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), i.e. the JDK provider for the default keystore type (e.g. SUN for pkcs12/jks), not a BouncyCastle provider as the CryptoProvider contract documents ("@return BouncyCastle security provider"). Any caller that trusts the contract—for example registering the result with Security.addProvider or using it for certificate/signature operations—will get the wrong provider and fail or behave unexpectedly. Since the authz-client has no BouncyCastle on its classpath, this method should return null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) or a genuine BC provider.

findings.title: AuthzClient.create now throws if no CryptoProvider is discoverable by its classloader
findings.body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). CryptoIntegration.init throws IllegalStateException("Not able to load any cryptoProvider with the classLoader ...") when no CryptoProvider SPI file is discoverable by that specific classloader. As a result, creating an AuthzClient now fails outright in environments where META-INF/services is not visible to AuthzClient's classloader (shaded/relocated jars, OSGi, custom classloaders), even though building the client does not otherwise need crypto. Previously create() worked without any crypto provider. This also adds an unexpected global static side effect to a simple factory method and should be made resilient to a missing provider.

findings.title: Core provider-selection change is untested
findings.body: ECDSAAlgorithmTest only round-trips a signature through the new ASN1 encoder/decoder; it never exercises the feature this PR introduces. There is no test that places two CryptoProvider service implementations on the classpath and asserts the highest-order provider is selected, no test that the previous duplicate-provider failure is (or is not) still raised for equal orders, and no test that an authz client obtains a usable crypto provider through CryptoIntegration after ServiceLoader discovery. Given the detectProvider behavior change, the selection logic—the main risk of the PR—has no coverage.

findings.title: getKeyStore ignores provider and cannot load non-JDK keystore formats
findings.body: getKeyStore(format) uses KeyStore.getInstance(format.name()) against the default JVM security providers instead of going through a specific provider. For formats the JDK does not ship (e.g. BCFKS, BKS, PEM) this throws KeyStoreException, so CryptoProvider.getSupportedKeyStoreTypes()/getKeyStore() will claim formats this provider cannot actually load, since the authz-client has no BouncyCastle on the classpath. It should throw UnsupportedOperationException for unsupported formats or otherwise limit to JDK-supported types.
